source: ACIAR AH/2005/086 'Smallholder Cattle Best Practice Manual' (Windsor, Bush & Young), Best Practice Health and Husbandry of Cattle, Cambodia -- hosted at mekonglivestock.wordpress.com (University of Sydney / GDAHP project site)
text: Recognising and reporting animal disease early is stressed as critical, since prompt reporting to a village animal health worker limits impact and economic loss, while delay risks prolonged sickness, death, and wider financial loss to the farmer, village, and beyond. Common warning signs listed include: the animal stops eating and drinking, lies down a lot, isolates itself from other animals, has discharge from eyes/nose/mouth, has diarrhoea or stops urinating/defecating, loses body condition or weight, has a rough coat, runs a fever (fast breathing, seeking cool areas), or dies suddenly. The manual lists simple, low-cost biosecurity measures any farmer or village can apply: vaccinate for high-impact diseases (FMD, HS, Blackleg); never bring unvaccinated new animals into the herd or village; quarantine any newly introduced animal (even if vaccinated) for 2-4 weeks in a separate area and observe daily; isolate sick animals from healthy ones and feed/handle them last with separate equipment; observe livestock daily and avoid contact with animals of unknown health status; only let breeding cattle mix with disease-free bulls and cows; avoid letting animals congregate with groups from other areas; and stay alert to local disease status, adjusting practices and consulting the VAHW or District Veterinarian when a threat is nearby.
